newsitem.title: USA: Dade Cty, Fla., $450 mln water-sewer deal delayed.
newsitem.headline: Dade Cty, Fla., $450 mln water-sewer deal delayed.

text.p: Dade County, Fla., delayed a $450 million water-sewer revenue bond issue due to market conditions, but expects the sale to proceed next week despite a pending lawsuit, a county official said Thursday.
Pricing was originally set for Jan 8 and 9.
"It is going next week," said Lidia Monzon-Aguirre, the county bond administrator. "Right now we're looking at prepricing Wednesday (Jan 15) for retail, with Thursday the institutional sale."
PaineWebber Inc is senior manager on the deal.
Miami bond dealer Leopoldo Guzman sued the Metro-Dade county government on Dec 26 after his firm, Guzman & Co, and another Miami firm, Howard Gary & Co, were removed from the underwriting team.

The lawsuit alleged that some county commissioners violated Florida's public meetings law by privately discussing the removal vote between the morning and afternoon sessions of the county commission meeting on Dec 17. Guzman sought an injunction blocking the bond sale.
County officials denied the allegation and said the commission acted legally.
On the morning of Dec 17, commissioners agreed in a 7-4 vote to a list of underwriters that included Gary and Guzman. They reversed themselves that afternoon and bumped the two firms in a 6-5 vote.
Howard Gary & Co was dismissed because of concerns about the role of its president, Howard Gary, as a government witness in a federal corruption probe of public finance in Miami and Dade County.

Commissioner Pedro Reboredo engineered the second vote, saying he had a change of heart and wanted Gary off the list because of public perception and because of fears that bond pricing could be affected.

County Commissioner Natacha Millan advocated Guzman's removal because of a letter circulated in November, accusing another firm that acts as a county financial adviser of violating municipal securities rules.
Guzman said the letter was a forgery and asked federal regulators to investigate. His attorney said Guzman passed a lie detector test.
Millan asked that Guzman be excluded because "there is a shadow cast upon this person." Guzman called the decision "arbitrary."

Guzman's lawsuit is still pending. Normally, the plaintiffs would have to wait 30 to 40 days to seek depositions from county commissioners about whether the vote was discussed outside the meeting, said Guzman's attorney, Richard Broksky.

Guzman's firm asked that the waiting period be waived. Circuit Judge Juan Ramirez said Wednesday he would deny the request, though he has yet to issue a written decision. Brodsky said he filed a brief asking the judge to reconsider. He said that if the request is granted, the depositions could be taken quickly enough that there would be no further delay in the bond sale unless there is evidence the vote was discussed privately.
"If they did, it would be a violation and the decision would be void from the beginning," Brodksy said.
Monzon-Aguirre said neither the lawsuit nor concerns about City of Miami finances were expected to hurt pricing.

"I think it'll be well received. I think the sophisticated investor knows the difference between Metro-Dade County and Miami," said Monzon-Aguirre. "We have proven that in the last several deals we have done."
Miami, the county seat, is struggling to close a $68 million deficit and is operating under a state oversight board. The county's finances and bond ratings have not been affected.
